scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that scandals can expose problems while arguing they are unreliable and harmful; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: A single scandal can dominate the news for weeks and seize everyone's attention.
Some people claim that scandals are useful because they focus our attention on problems as no speaker or reformer ever could.
I agree that scandals can expose real problems, but I do not believe they are a reliably useful way to do so.
First, scandals really can force public attention onto serious problems.
A shocking event often makes people notice an issue they had long ignored.
For example, a scandal about unsafe products can suddenly push a government to pass stronger laws.
This shows that scandals can achieve change that quiet warnings never managed.
Public outrage can give reformers the energy they need to fix a hidden wrong.
A dramatic scandal can reveal problems that powerful people had worked hard to hide.
To this extent, scandals can indeed be useful.
Second, however, scandals are an unreliable and often harmful way to highlight problems.
Attention drawn by a scandal usually focuses on shocking people rather than on real solutions.
Consider how a scandal can ruin an innocent person's reputation before the facts are even clear.
Such damage shows that scandals can harm as much as they help.
The public also tends to forget a scandal as soon as the next one appears.
Important but undramatic problems may be ignored simply because they create no scandal.
Scandals, then, are a clumsy and unreliable tool for solving real problems.
In conclusion, scandals can sometimes force useful attention onto hidden problems.
But they are unreliable and often harmful, focusing on shock rather than on solutions.
Real progress depends far more on steady reform than on the passing storm of a scandal.
